raw_prompt: Can you write a short introduction about the relevance of the term "monopsony" in economics? Please use examples related to potential monopsonies in the labour market and cite relevant research.
prompt_sent: Can you write a short introduction about the relevance of the term "monopsony" in economics? Please use examples related to potential monopsonies in the labour market and cite relevant research.
response_text:
Monopsony is the buyer-side analogue of monopoly: instead of one seller having power over many buyers, one employer, or a small group of employers, has power over many workers. Joan Robinson introduced the term in *The Economics of Imperfect Competition* as a way to describe buyer power, and the classic textbook example is a firm that is the dominant buyer of labour in an isolated town. Its relevance in economics is that wages may then reflect not only workers’ productivity, but also workers’ limited outside options.

In labour markets, monopsony need not mean there is literally only one employer. Modern “monopsony” often refers to imperfect competition caused by search frictions, commuting costs, licensing barriers, non-compete clauses, job-specific skills, care responsibilities, immigration constraints, or simple employer concentration. Alan Manning’s *Monopsony in Motion* argues that when workers cannot instantly move to equivalent jobs, firms face an upward-sloping labour supply curve and can set wages below marginal product without losing their entire workforce. This makes monopsony central to debates on minimum wages, antitrust policy, collective bargaining, inequality, and the labour share of income.

Potential examples include hospital systems in local healthcare labour markets, where mergers can reduce outside options for specialized workers. Prager and Schmitt find that hospital mergers slowed wage growth when the merger substantially increased local employer concentration and when workers’ skills were specific to hospitals. Another example is concentrated local hiring in particular occupations: Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum show that many U.S. labour markets, defined by occupation and commuting zone, are highly concentrated, suggesting that workers in some places face only a few serious potential employers. More generally, evidence that firms differ in wage-setting power, even for similar workers, links monopsony to wage inequality; Card, Cardoso, Heining, and Kline review evidence that firm-level wage policies matter for inequality, while Azar, Berry, and Marinescu estimate substantial labour-market power using online job-application data. Policy-oriented work by Naidu, Posner, and Weyl therefore treats labour monopsony as an antitrust problem as well as a labour-market problem.

A useful short framing is: monopsony matters because labour markets are often “thin” or frictional, so employers may have discretion over pay. Where workers cannot easily switch jobs, employer concentration, mergers, restrictive contracts, or platform control can suppress wages, reduce mobility, and make employment outcomes differ from the competitive benchmark.

**References**

- Azar, José, Steven T. Berry, and Ioana Marinescu. 2022. “Estimating Labor Market Power.” NBER Working Paper No. 30365. https://www.nber.org/papers/w30365  
- Azar, José, Ioana Marinescu, and Marshall Steinbaum. 2022. “Labor Market Concentration.” *Journal of Human Resources* 57(S): S167-S199. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.monopsony.1218-9914R1  
- Card, David, Ana Rute Cardoso, Jörg Heining, and Patrick Kline. 2018. “Firms and Labor Market Inequality: Evidence and Some Theory.” *Journal of Labor Economics* 36(S1): S13-S70. https://www.iza.org/publications/dp/9850/firms-and-labor-market-inequality-evidence-and-some-theory  
- Manning, Alan. 2003. *Monopsony in Motion: Imperfect Competition in Labor Markets*. Princeton University Press. https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691123285/monopsony-in-motion  
- Manning, Alan. 2021. “Monopsony in Labor Markets: A Review.” *ILR Review* 74(1): 3-26. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0019793920922499  
- Naidu, Suresh, Eric A. Posner, and E. Glen Weyl. 2018. “Antitrust Remedies for Labor Market Power.” *Harvard Law Review* 132: 536-601. https://harvardlawreview.org/print/vol-132/antitrust-remedies-for-labor-market-power/  
- Prager, Elena, and Matt Schmitt. 2021. “Employer Consolidation and Wages: Evidence from Hospitals.” *American Economic Review* 111(2): 397-427. https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20190690
